title: One Fate, So Live Fully Now
overview: Because death comes to good and bad people alike, the Teacher urges readers to enjoy life and act while they can, even though wisdom often goes unrewarded.

parts.label: The same end for all (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The Teacher concludes that the righteous and the wise, and what they do, are in God's hands, yet no one can tell from how life goes whether love or hate awaits them. Good and bad, religious and careless, all meet the same death, and he calls this the evil running through everything, made worse by the madness in human hearts.

parts.label: Better a live dog (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: Dogs were despised scavengers and lions were admired, yet the lowest living creature still has hope that the greatest dead one does not. Here the dead are pictured as cut off from knowing, loving or being remembered, a bleak view that reflects how much of the Old Testament speaks of death, before clearer hopes of resurrection developed.

parts.label: Enjoy your days (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: White clothes and oil on the head were signs of celebration and comfort, so the advice is to eat, drink, love your spouse and live joyfully as a gift from God. Work hard at whatever is in front of you, because Sheol, the shadowy place of the dead, holds no more work or plans.

parts.label: Time and chance (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: The fastest, strongest and smartest do not always win, because timing and circumstance shape every life. Like fish caught in a net, people are often caught off guard by sudden disaster.

parts.label: The forgotten wise man (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: In this example a poor man's wisdom saves a small city from a powerful king, yet no one remembers him afterward. Christians have sometimes read this forgotten rescuer as a picture of Jesus, though the passage itself does not say so.

parts.label: Quiet wisdom, fragile good (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: Calm words from a wise person are worth more than a foolish ruler's shouting, and wisdom beats weapons. Yet it is easily ignored, and one wrongdoer can undo a great deal of good.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the bleak view of death in verses 2 to 10 is the Teacher's own considered wisdom, an honest view limited to life "under the sun," or a skeptic's outlook that the book raises in order to answer it.
think: If good and bad people often end up with the same outcomes, what, if anything, still makes it worth trying to live well?
